title: Feedback
primary_metric: worst-case gain-before-feedback score (dB), the minimum GBF value across the verse position and both ends of the bridge cross, for each candidate wedge position

options.A: Commit the lead vocal wedge to House-Left — closer to the mic's on-axis line, but farther away (6, 5 ft)
options.B: Commit the lead vocal wedge to House-Right — much closer to the mic, but almost directly off to its side (0, 6 ft)

sources.placeholder: Appendix B — cardioid microphone polar equation and reference dB points
sources.claim: The cardioid microphone polar pattern equation, and real measured reference points confirming it
sources.value: g(theta) = 0.5(1 + cos theta); measured points 0 dB at 0 deg, 3 dB rejection at ~65.5 deg, 6 dB rejection at 90 deg, >20 dB (in practice) at 180 deg
sources.as_of: current as of access; DPA dictionary entry is not dated but describes standard, static acoustic theory
sources.title: "Cardioid Microphone" — DPA Microphones Mic University dictionary entry
sources.note: A working professional microphone manufacturer's own published technical dictionary entry, fetched directly. The idealized formula's prediction at 65.5 deg (20*log10(0.5*(1+cos(65.5deg))) = 3.0 dB) matches the source's own independently stated measured reference point exactly, which is used in case.md as an explicit validation, not merely an assertion.

sources.placeholder: Appendix D — mechanism of gain-before-feedback (distance and directivity)
sources.claim: Gain-before-feedback depends on the inverse-square-law distance effect (6 dB per doubling/halving of mic-to-source distance) and on aiming a directional mic's least-sensitive angle at the loudspeaker
sources.value: 6 dB per halving of distance; directional mics aimed so pattern is weakest toward the loudspeaker
sources.units: dB per distance-halving; qualitative directivity guidance
sources.as_of: current as of access; general encyclopedia article, not dated to a specific edition
sources.title: "Gain before feedback"
sources.note: General encyclopedia entry, not peer-reviewed or a manufacturer source, but states an uncontested, standard piece of acoustics (inverse square law applied to gain-before-feedback) corroborated independently by S3's PAG formula structure. This case applies the stated source-to-mic distance rule to a mic-to-loudspeaker (monitor) distance instead -- the same physics of a point source's SPL falling off with distance, not a different claim.

sources.placeholder: Appendix D — general structure of a real potential-acoustic-gain calculation
sources.claim: The general structure of a real potential-acoustic-gain (PAG) calculation: a 20*log10 distance-ratio term plus separate additive directivity and open-mic-count terms
sources.value: 20*log10((D0*Ds)/(D1*D2)) distance-ratio structure; separate additive pattern-directivity term (0 to +8 dB); separate additive open-mic penalty (~ -3 dB per doubling of open mics, via a 10*log rule)
sources.title: "Gain Before Feedback Calculator for Live Sound"
sources.note: A trade/hobbyist audio publication, not peer-reviewed or a manufacturer source. Used only to independently confirm the *shape* of a real PAG-style calculation (a log-distance term plus additive directivity/open-mic terms) against S2 -- no specific numeric value from this source is used as a load-bearing figure anywhere in this case's own GBF score, which is a simplified two-term version built for the two factors that actually differ between House-Left and House-Right (SEE case.md Appendix D, MA4).

deliverables.text: A rectangular-to-polar conversion table for House-Left and House-Right: position (x,y) converted to (r, theta) measured off the mic's on-axis heading, full conversion shown.
A graph of the microphone's cardioid polar equation over a full revolution, with both wedges' theta marked and their pattern-rejection dB values labeled.
The performer's cross written as parametric equations x(t), y(t); the parameter eliminated to find the rectangular equation of her path; used to find where she crosses the fixed follow-spot line y=2.
A gain-before-feedback table at every checked blocking moment (verse, cross-start, cross-end) for both wedges: distance term, pattern-rejection term, combined GBF score, arithmetic shown.
A final decision table: each wedge's single worst (lowest) GBF moment and the margin between the two wedges at their worst moments, with a stated recommendation.

appendices.title: The Stage Plot and the Two Wedge Positions

balance.argument_a: House-Left's worst checked moment is the end of the bridge cross (mic at (0,3), House-Left at (6,5)): r=6.325 ft, theta=18.43 deg off-axis, GBF = 16.246 dB. That is House-Left's floor across every checked blocking moment (static verse 18.923 dB, cross-start 16.427 dB, cross-end 16.246 dB).
balance.argument_b: House-Right's worst checked moment is also the end of the bridge cross (mic at (0,3), House-Right at (0,6)): r=3.000 ft, theta=90.00 deg off-axis, GBF = 15.563 dB. That is House-Right's floor across every checked blocking moment (static verse 21.584 dB, cross-start 24.677 dB, cross-end 15.563 dB). House-Right's static-verse number alone looks far safer (21.584 vs 18.923, a 14.1% naive edge) -- but the bridge cross brings the mic much closer to House-Right than to House-Left, which is what actually governs.
balance.margin_basis: Compare each wedge's single worst (lowest) GBF score across all three checked moments: (16.246 - 15.563) / 15.563 = 4.39%. House-Left is the safer overall recommendation by this margin, despite losing badly on the static-verse-only comparison -- the trap is stopping the analysis at the verse.
balance.twist_effect: A closing tableau mark at (1,4) ft, revealed only during the Socratic discussion (not in the student packet), is checked as a fourth moment. House-Left's GBF there is 14.235 dB -- worse than its prior floor of 16.246 dB, and now the lowest number either wedge posts anywhere in the case. House-Right's GBF at the same point is 18.159 dB, above its own existing floor of 15.563 dB (unchanged). The verdict flips: House-Right becomes the safer recommendation by 9.33%. Verified mechanically by evaluate_twist() in sensitivity_model.py. Honest caveat: the flip depends on the tableau mark landing closer to House-Left's exposure than House-Right's; a tableau mark placed instead near House-Right would reinforce the pre-twist verdict rather than overturn it.
balance.stability: NOT stable under a +/-50% flex of MA1 (wedge coordinates) and MA3 (cross coordinates): house_left_x -50%, house_left_y -50%, house_right_y +50%, and cross_end_y -50% each flip the base winner from House-Left to House-Right, at flexed margins of roughly 16%-33%. This is disclosed, not hidden -- the base margin (4.39%) is thin because the two wedges are a genuinely close call, and case.md Appendix E already names MA1 and MA3 as load-bearing without stating the flip threshold or direction. See sensitivity_disclosure[] below.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: The Ridgeline Playhouse is fictional (case.md Background, Appendix E MA1); House-Left's exact stage coordinates are the case's own stated scenario numbers, not a knowable real-world given. Flexed -50% (from x=6 to x=3), the base verdict flips to House-Right at a 30.77% margin; flexed +50% (x=9) the base verdict A does not flip but the margin widens to 20.29%, just past the SPEC §2 cap. Already disclosed in FACILITATOR.md's Facilitator-only numbers and in case.json.balance.stability, and explored directly with students via Anchor 4 and Socratic question 4.

Same basis as house_left_x -- House-Left's stage coordinates are MA1's fictional scenario numbers. Flexed -50% (from y=5 to y=2.5), the base verdict flips to House-Right at a 20.70% margin. Already disclosed in FACILITATOR.md's Facilitator-only numbers and in case.json.balance.stability.

Same basis as house_left_x/y -- House-Right's stage coordinates are MA1's fictional scenario numbers. Flexed +50% (house_right_y from 6 to 9 ft), the base verdict flips to House-Right at a 32.85% margin. Flexed -50% degenerates to a monitor coincident with the cross-end mic position (r=0), reported by sensitivity_model.py as an unbounded worst case rather than masked -- a real, if extreme, reading of what 'the monitor sits exactly where the performer stands' means.

Dana's cross-end mark (MA3) is the case's own fictional choreography. Flexed -50% (from y=3 to y=1.5), the base verdict flips to House-Right at a 16.18% margin -- the single most sensitive dial in the case alongside the House-Left coordinates, and exactly why case.md's MA3 sensitivity column says the answer is sensitive to this value without stating which direction it moves.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: House-Left and House-Right wedge positions (Appendix A)
modeling_assumptions.value_used: (6, 5) ft and (0, 6) ft, in the mic's own reference frame
modeling_assumptions.basis: The Ridgeline Playhouse is a fictional venue; there is no real stage plot to source. The two positions are dimensioned to be realistic for a small community-theater stage -- a handful of feet from a center-stage mic stand, one noticeably farther but more forward, one noticeably closer but nearly abeam -- and were not chosen to make either option obviously better by eye.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: The comparison between the two wedges depends directly on these four coordinates. A different real stage plot would give different exact numbers; that dependency is disclosed here, not hidden.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: The mic's on-axis heading is held fixed throughout the whole number, including while Dana is handheld and moving
modeling_assumptions.value_used: applied to the static verse and the entire bridge cross
modeling_assumptions.basis: A real performer's handheld mic technique varies; holding the heading fixed is what makes a single, stated stage-plot reference frame valid for every position in this case, matching a real director's blocking note to keep the mic aimed out during a cross.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: If a performer instead re-aimed the mic to face the audience at every instant, every angle in Appendices C and D would change with her heading, not just her position -- a materially different and much harder case. This case's whole geometry depends on MA2 holding.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Dana's bridge-cross start point, end point, and duration (Appendix C)
modeling_assumptions.basis: Both the venue and the number are fictional, so there is no real blocking script to source. Values dimensioned to be a realistic few-foot cross completed within one musical phrase of a mid-tempo number.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: The specific worst-case GBF moment for each wedge -- and therefore which wedge wins -- depends on these four numbers. The answer is sensitive to this value, which is exactly why D4 checks every blocking mark rather than assuming the static verse position is the whole story.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Priya checks GBF only at named blocking marks, not continuously, and treats the room/loudspeaker/open-mic count as identical between wedges tonight
modeling_assumptions.basis: A live engineer preps fader moves for the marks a director actually calls, not for an unbounded number of in-between instants; tonight's room, PA, and mic count genuinely do not change based on which wedge is chosen.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Narrows the case to a tractable, real engineering practice; does not by itself favor either wedge, since both are checked at the same set of moments.

sensitivity_note: SPEC §6 does not apply -- no illness, death, or financial-hardship stakes. Mild ordinary stage-production tension only (a show that could be interrupted by feedback squeal), not flagged.

cohort_bands.note: The Socratic plan and anchor timings in FACILITATOR.md run as written (0:00-45:00). Split the room into two desks for the Data Deep Dive -- one works House-Left's numbers, one works House-Right's -- and have them trade tables before D5. Run both deep-conflict threads.

Anchors 2 and 3 combine into one pass ('what are we actually measuring, and at which moments'). Run one deep-conflict thread only -- the static-vs-worst-case trap, which needs the least setup. The twist still drops at 15:00. Do not split into two desks; work one wedge's numbers together on the board and let the other be homework. Total runtime about 30 minutes.

There is no vote to take at Anchor 1 -- the learner states an initial position instead of a hands-up split, and the guide argues the other wedge directly rather than cold-calling. The twist still lands, but 'who reverses' becomes 'would you reverse, and why'. Skip the deep-conflict threads and go from the twist recommit straight to Close, spending the recovered time on D3's parameter elimination, the single hardest algebra step to do alone.

catalog.ask: One working monitor circuit, a stage cross mid-song, and a live mic that's one wrong angle away from a full-volume squeal in front of a sold-out house. The wedge position that looks safest standing still might not be the one that survives the choreography.
